#6185. Would Alaska-Hawaiian 12-Year Widebody Captains Really Earn $493.41 An Hour Under The Tentative Pilot Contract?

Tada Images | Shutterstock, Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying

After more than 600 days of negotiations, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines came to a tentative Joint Collective Bargaining Agreement with the Air Line Pilots Association International (ALPA). The terms now dictate that a 12-year widebody captain will earn an eye-popping base rate of $493.41 an hour starting in early 2027. Most mainline airline pilots credit between 800 and 1,000 flight hours per year, meaning a $493.41 rate translates to roughly $395,000 to $493,000 in base flight pay.

That rate is only the starting point for 2027 and is scheduled to rise annually, reaching $539.16 per hour by 2030, according to Aero Crew News. The Black Box Aviation Podcast reported that rates will be adjusted annually to match the average of American, Delta, Southwest, and United on comparable aircraft, or increase by at least 3%, whichever is greater. Alaska Air Group will also contribute 18% directly to 401(k) accounts, alongside a performance-based program with 5% annual payouts.

The terms ALPA agreed to on November 10 will be put to a vote on December 1 for the 4,600 union membersto collectively ratify, according to Airline Geeks. If approved, the new pay scales take effect on January 31, 2027. The new contract represents an immediate raise from $86.41 to $102.41 per hour, or a 21.2% to 26.2% pay bump.

The agreement is a long-awaited resolution following Alaska Air Group’s $1.9 billion acquisition of Hawaiian in September 2024. While the Federal Aviation Administration approved the financial merger and granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, aircrews remained divided. Formal joint negotiations launched in February 2025, aiming not only to set uniform pay rates but also to establish an operational framework to reorganize the pilots and jets of the combined fleet.

ALPA negotiators built the new agreement on Alaska’s existing contract framework while preserving legacy Hawaiian protections. Until the unified labor contract is official, management cannot freely assign pilots across both of the newly combined networks or readily swap aircraft to new airfields based on changing demand.

Captain Drew Coyle, the Alaska Airlines MEC chair, commented on the negotiations.

“Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex issues facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”

The tentative agreement also clears a major labor hurdle to Alaska’s long-haul expansion and Hawaiian's $600 million modernization plan. Alaska is expecting up to 17 new Boeing 787 Dreamliners that will launch 12 new overseas routes. Meanwhile, Hawaiian’s fleet overhaul in Honolulu will retrofit all 24 Airbus A330-200 widebodies with new Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Still, flying two dozen midlife A330s alongside new 787s forces the airline to maintain separate supply chains, training programs, and maintenance programs.

Passing this contract is only half the battle because Alaska and Hawaiian pilots still cannot fly each other's jets until their seniority lists merge. Under federal law, a neutral arbitrator must combine both pilot rosters into a single master list. Because seniority controls everything from captain upgrades to holiday schedules, pilots must stay separated on their legacy fleets until that process finishes.

Before seniority talks even wrap up, all 4,600 member pilots must approve the four-year agreement itself. Union voting runs from December 1 through December 22. If a majority votes yes, the new pay rates and scheduling rules officially take effect on January 31, 2027, locking in labor stability through January 30, 2031, while eliminating the old pay gap between both workforces.

Captain Larry Payne, the Hawaiian Airlines MEC chair, also remarked on the agreement.

“This joint collective bargaining agreement represents an important milestone for both pilot groups. The decisions made throughout these negotiations will shape our pilots’ careers and quality of life for years to come. If approved, this agreement will establish the foundation for future contracts as we move forward together as one pilot group.”

Once seniority lists finally combine, Alaska Air Group can unleash the full scheduling flexibility it bought with the merger. Management will be able to shift crews seamlessly between Hawaii's refreshed narrowbodies and Seattle's growing Dreamliner fleet as seasonal travel shifts. That operational freedom was impossible after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted a single operating certificate in October 2025, merging safety rules but leaving cockpits divided.

Ultimately, locking in $493.41 an hour for widebody captains proves Alaska is serious about competing alongside major legacy airlines on global routes. Yet paying top-tier wages across both fleets raises the stakes for every flight across the Pacific. The carrier's long-term financial success now hinges on whether it can fill those upgraded cabins at profitable fares against tough domestic and international rivals.

Executives cite disproportionate overhead and geopolitical fuel shocks as they realign post merger operations and roles.

As part of the merger, Alaska took over Hawaiian's 787 Dreamliner orders and rebranded its existing 787s to construct an international gateway at its historic Seattle-Tacoma International (SEA) base. To make the increased $493.41 widebody pay rate financially viable, Alaska is dividing its twin-aisle jets across the combined fleet's two unique hubs. Thus, Hawaiian maintains its legacy A330-200s in Honolulu to meet established island leisure and regional Pacific demand.

Hawaiian originally sought the 787-9 in 2018 to upgrade its fleet and increase capacity on long-haul Pacific routes. Hawaiian even canceled a prior order for six A330neos because the Dreamliner had superior fuel efficiency, longer range, and more business-class seating in densely populated markets such as Tokyo and New York. Hawaiian eventually increased its commitment to 12 Dreamliners before merging with Alaska.

Alaska now has widebody jets, experienced pilots, and foreign operating certificates, which it lacked as a primarily narrowbody airline before acquiring Hawaiian. From Seattle, Alaska deploys the 787-9 on ultra-long, high-demand routes to Tokyo Narita, Seoul, London, Rome, Paris, and Athens. The Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency are an ideal fit for these business and luxury travel corridors where higher ticket prices offset premium pilot wages.

In January, Alaska placed a historic order for 105 737 MAX 10s and five more 787-10s, pushing its total Boeing order book past 240 planes. This international push fits naturally with the airline's identity as a fiercely loyal, all-Boeing mainline operator based in Boeing’s backyard. By folding Hawaiian’s Dreamliners into an all-Boeing fleet, Alaska avoids the high cost of training crews and stocking parts for Airbus widebodies.

Back in Honolulu, Hawaiian’s A330-200 fleet anchors core flights to Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, Sydney, Papeete, and Pago Pago, alongside major West Coast cities. Starting in 2028, Hawaiian will upgrade all 24 jets with new Leihōkū lie-flat suites and premium economy cabins. Although older A330s lack the Dreamliner’s range and fuel efficiency, their lower ownership costs bring costs down to make economy vacation airfare more affordable.

Apart from this change, today will also see the airline finally join Alaska Airlines in the oneworld alliance.

The narrowbody crews of the combined Alaska-Hawaiian fleet are about to undergo a significant fleet makeover, much like the widebody pilots who fly long ocean trips. Hawaiian is retiring its outdated 717s, which are frequently used for interisland flights between Honolulu and nearby islands. As part of the expanded narrowbody business in the continental US, Alaska Air Group is moving some 737-800s to Hawaii and bringing its own new 737 MAX 8 and MAX 10 aircraft.

Under the new deal, 12-year narrowbody captains are paid $401.09 per hour. That's $92.32 less than widebody captains. Despite the lower hourly pay, narrowbody pilots perform significantly more takeoffs and landings every shift. This is especially true for crews doing 30-minute island hops. Replacing the 128-seat 717 with larger 737s will add dozens of additional seats per flight while also updating the flight deck, saving fuel on each sortie, and decreasing fleet maintenance. The pilots will have to train on a larger airframe, but the airline will be able to transport more passengers without recruiting additional workers.

Switching to an all-737 narrowbody fleet simplifies pilot training and spare parts across both airlines. Instead of maintaining separate cockpit ratings for 717s, A321neos, and 737s, pilots can eventually fly a single narrowbody type across West Coast and island routes. This standardization lets management smoothly shift crews between mainland and island flying whenever seasonal travel demand spikes or dips.

Still, operating larger 737s on short interisland routes brings clear economic and mechanical trade-offs. Because the 737-800 is much heavier than the 717, it burns more fuel per trip and puts extra wear on brakes and landing gear during frequent landings. However, the higher seat capacity lowers the cost per passenger, helping the airline offset those added baseline expenses.

#6182. JetBlue Doubles Down In Fort Lauderdale With New Flights To Grand Cayman & Honduras In 2027

JetBlue Airways announced two new daily international services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) on Thursday, connecting South Florida with Grand Cayman and Tegucigalpa in Honduras starting in February 2027. The airline says its latest move will expand its international network at the airport to 20 destinations, strengthening its position as a gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean.

These latest additions follow Spirit Airlines' collapse in May, which created substantial opportunities at its former Fort Lauderdale stronghold. JetBlue has moved aggressively to capture displaced demand, with an analysis of Department of Transportation (DOT) data revealing that the airline's international passenger traffic is growing even faster than its added capacity.

The first new service will launch on February 23, connecting Fort Lauderdale with Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman. Two days later, JetBlue will begin flying to Palmerola International Airport (XPL) in Comayagua, serving the Honduran capital, Tegucigalpa. Both routes will operate daily using Airbus A220 and A320 family aircraft, with introductory one-way fares starting at $99 and $183, respectively.

The Honduras route will be JetBlue's first service to the Tegucigalpa area, complementing its existing San Pedro Sula operation. Daniel Shurz, JetBlue's Senior Vice President of Network Planning, emphasized the airline's commitment to expanding international connectivity and providing more options for travelers visiting friends and relatives.

"We're grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we're committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they're looking for. With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we're strengthening Fort Lauderdale's role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean."

Grand Cayman represents a return following JetBlue's short-lived service introduced in December 2025. The airline will also offer temporary daily flights to Port of Spain between January 29 and February 15 for Trinidad and Tobago's Carnival. Following the recent launch of new routes to Barranquilla and Cali, Colombia, JetBlue expects to exceed 150 daily departures at FLL during winter peaks, its largest schedule ever.

JetBlue's international expansion at Fort Lauderdale has been substantial. An analysis of DOT T-100 International Segment data (available through August) shows the airline offered almost 1.7 million international seats in the first eight months of this year, up 33.4% year-on-year. The growth reflects an increasingly diverse network, with new and restored routes complementing established Caribbean and Latin American services.

Much of the additional capacity stems from six international routes launched or restored in December 2025, including Aruba, Cartagena, Grand Cayman, Liberia, San Pedro Sula, and Sint Maarten. Meanwhile, Guayaquil, Guatemala City, and Santiago have also seen significant growth, showing how JetBlue has strengthened previously limited operations.

However, growth has not been uniform. Montego Bay experienced a 33.9% capacity reduction, while Kingston, Cancún, and Punta Cana also recorded declines. The expansion has also coincided with international route reductions elsewhere in its network. The net result is that JetBlue is not only growing its FLL international network but also diversifying it and concentrating capacity where opportunities are strongest.

JetBlue’s latest growth spurt cements its rise as Fort Lauderdale’s new number one airline.

Although JetBlue's international expansion at FLL was already underway before Spirit's demise on May 2, the vacuum left by its former competitor has given it the space to accelerate that growth. To assess performance after Spirit's exit, Simple Flying zoomed in on DOT T-100 data for May-August, compared with the same period last year.

The findings are striking. JetBlue has increased its international seat capacity by 33.0%, yet passenger traffic surged by 45.8%, lifting average load factors from 79.4% to 87.0%, an improvement of 7.6 percentage points. For context, Delta Air Lines averages about 85% load factors on its international routes, and at 87%, Fort Lauderdale is the top-performing base in JetBlue's network.

This clearly demonstrates that JetBlue has not yet reached the limits of demand at Fort Lauderdale, because even as it adds more capacity, it is attracting even more passengers and filling a greater proportion of those seats. And there is the knock-on effect: Growing international passenger volumes also increase ancillary revenues, with JetBlue reporting 20% year-on-year loyalty revenue growth in Q3 2026, alongside a 55% increase in co-branded credit card acquisitions in South Florida.

A larger international network will certainly reinforce those trends. However, the airline's longer-term success will depend on translating this rapid passenger growth into stronger yields and sustainable commercial returns.

#6181. Southwest Signs Interline Deal With French Bee

Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

#6179. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6177. What Air Force One Pilots Do Before Flights That Most Other Pilots Never Do

Standard actions for a commercial airline crew before a flight include reviewing the flight with each other, followed by a pre-flight walkaround. Later, the crew sets up the flight deck, inputs their flight plan into the aircraft's computer, and verifies the aircraft's weight and balance figures before pushback. It's a thorough procedure to ensure the aircraft is fully ready to operate safely, and these procedures apply to essentially every commercial flight.

The pilots of Air Force One also do these actions, but their pre-flight duties are much more thorough because of their job: transporting the President of the United States. Air Force One is a callsign used to denote any US Air Force (USAF) aircraft flying the President, but it is most commonly associated with two Boeing VC-25As and the VC-25B Bridge, which are based on the Boeing 747. Crucially, the flight crew is concerned not just with safety, but also with security.

The two VC-25As are typically flown by two pilots, a flight engineer, and a navigator, while the VC-25B Bridge does not require a flight engineer (because it's based on the newer 747-8). Before each flight, they coordinate with ground crews to verify that the apron and runway are clear of potential debris. The flight plan itself may look significantly different from what airliners operate, and the crew also needs to ensure that the aircraft's onboard security and defense systems are operational.

In addition to these actions, the flight crew of Air Force One needs to help maintain security. This means not just coordinating with security teams on the apron, but also with air traffic control to ensure that the airport and surrounding airspace is clear of any potential conflicts. The crew also verifies that the aircraft will receive priority handling from air traffic control, and they also must review aerial refueling procedures for the VC-25A, although this capability has never been used with the president onboard.

The pilots typically must arrive three to four hours before the scheduled flight, coordinating with the US Secret Service to maintain security on the aircraft and at the airport. The aircraft is inspected, and its systems are tested to check for any potential technical faults. In addition, the crew has to review emergency procedures while also performing the more typical actions that you'd expect during the pre-flight flow. While this is usually a multi-hour process, flight crews are trained to perform departures with as little as an hour's notice.

Every long-distance trip undertaken by the US president begins and ends at the White House South Lawn. Here, the president boards a US Marine Corps helicopter operating under the callsign 'Marine One', the callsign used for any USMC aircraft carrying the US president. The helicopter, which may be joined by several others during the trip, flies to Andrews Air Force Base, home to the Presidential Airlift Group. The flight typically takes about six to ten minutes, and when the president lands, Air Force One is already waiting.

The VC-25s not only carry the president, but they also transport the president's Secret Service detail, senior staff, medical personnel, and advisors. In addition, the aircraft will typically carry the White House press pool, a rotating group of reporters and journalists covering the president. The president is always the last person to board the aircraft, and once he/she is onboard, the doors close before the engines are started. From there, the aircraft taxis to the runway and takes off.

Upon arrival, the airport receiving Air Force One typically suspends operations. From there, the president may either take a motorcade or another US Marine Corps helicopter to their final destination. The vehicles required for the motorcade and the USMC helicopters are typically flown in ahead of time via a Lockheed C-5 Galaxy to ensure that they're ready for the president's arrival. When it's time to return to Washington, this process repeats itself.

A former Air Force official claimed there wasn’t enough time to equip the aircraft with all of the “normal” modifications.

The pilots commanding the VC-25s must be experienced airmen serving with the US Air Force. Generally, these crew members have prior experience operating complex multi-engine transport aircraft and must have logged a significant number of flight hours (generally at least 2,500 hours). From there, pilots usually transfer to the 89th Airlift Wing at Andrews Air Force Base and build experience transporting other executives on aircraft like the Boeing C-32 or C-40 Clipper.

Pilots must maintain an exemplary flying record while serving in the USAF and keep a spotless permanent record. In addition, they must earn high-level qualifications to stand out further. Senior leadership evaluates the pilot roster at the 89th Airlift Wing, then handpicks the top aviators to enter the selection process for the Presidential Airlift Group. From there, the selection process includes interviews, psychological screenings, and simulator tests.

The final piece for those selected to pilot the VC-25 is to obtain 'Yankee White' clearance. This is a special, top-level security clearance reserved for personnel supporting the US president and vice president, and getting it requires an extremely thorough background check. Investigators may interview family members and peers, as well as former neighbors or teachers to verify stability, loyalty, and dependability, in a process that can take as long as a year. Candidates must also have a spotless criminal and financial history.

The VC-25As that commonly serve as Air Force One are designed to serve as invulnerable command centers in the sky. They feature advanced defense and communications systems, while also being equipped with aerial refueling systems so that they may remain airborne until food and water run out. However, the 747-based VC-25As are also massive aircraft. Not every airport can easily accommodate the VC-25As, and they draw a huge amount of attention, which isn't always ideal.

While the VC-25As are the most common aircraft that serve as Air Force One, the US president also occasionally travels on the Boeing C-32A, based on the 757-200. These planes are generally used when the president is traveling to airfields that cannot accommodate the VC-25A, and they can also be used as a backup aircraft when the president travels, as well as if a VC-25A is unavailable. Furthermore, the C-32s are useful when the president is traveling on sensitive missions, such as to active war zones.

In February 2023, former president Joe Biden secretly traveled to Ukraine, marking the first time in modern history that a US president had visited an active war zone not under the control of the US. To get there, he took a C-32A rather than the VC-25A, stopping at Ramstein Air Base in Germany for refueling before proceeding to Poland, where he boarded a train to Ukraine. The C-32 was preferable because of the sensitivity of the mission, and the flight didn't even use the standard Air Force One callsign in this case; rather, the callsign used was 'SAM060'.

A review of the differences between the older B747-200 vs the older VC-25A Air Force One (AFO). Then review the newer B747-8i vs the new VC-25B AFO.

The two VC-25As were delivered in the early 1990s and are based on the 747-200B, an aircraft that first entered service in the early 1970s. They're old and increasingly unreliable, and maintaining these aircraft is becoming difficult and expensive. As such, the USAF selected the 747-8 to serve as the platform for the replacement VC-25B in 2015, with first delivery scheduled for 2024. However, this has been pushed back multiple times, with first delivery now targeted for 2028.

In 2025, the US government accepted a 747-8 configured as a business jet from the Qatari government as a gift. This aircraft, now titled the VC25B Bridge, is intended to serve as an interim supplement for the existing VC-25A fleet until the two VC-25Bs are ready. The focus with the VC-25B Bridge was to get the aircraft ready as soon as possible, and it entered service in July 2026, less than a year after it was accepted. The catch is that it lacks many of the safety and defense features that are typically needed for the missions.

The VC-25B Bridge is only intended to be in service until the VC-25Bs arrive, and the aircraft is set to be retired before the end of President Donald Trump's second term. The VC-25Bs that will succeed it are conversions of whitetail aircraft, but they are being retrofitted with a full assortment of security, communications, and defensive technologies. Not only will they replace the VC-25B Bridge, but they will also replace the VC-25As, and they will be among the world's most advanced and secure aircraft in service.

#6176. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6175. How Much Does It Cost To Earn United Premier 1K Status In 2026?

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

United Airlines' MileagePlus program launched on May 6, 1981, according to The Points Guy. The program, which celebrated its 45th anniversary this year, has undergone many iterations, particularly after the 2010 merger with Continental Airlines. According to NerdWallet, the program's most recent change took place on April 2, fine-tuning the mile-earning schedule for today's economy. Basic Economy officially no longer earns travelers miles, and it has reduced miles per dollar earned at each status level.

Premier 1K, United's top tier of earned status for passengers, grants a variety of benefits, amenities, and privileges onboard and in the airport. Premier 1K unlocks United's most comprehensive set of publicly available elite benefits, including priority pre-boarding, complimentary Premier Upgrades cleared as early as 96 hours before departure, three free checked bags, Economy Plus seating at booking for the member and up to eight companions, access to expanded award availability, a dedicated Premier phone line, and a bonus of 280 PlusPoints that can be used to request upgrades on eligible flights.

There are two main ways to achieve such status, including flying on United or United Express operated flights in a class other than Basic Economy, and with credit card spending with United's co-branded Chase credit card lineup. The exclusivity comes at a price, and not just anyone may qualify for Premier 1K, let alone United's entry level status, Premier Silver. For the 2026 qualification year, United Airlines illustrates on its website that earning Premier 1K status requires either 28,000 Premier Qualifying Points (PQP) or a combination of 22,000 PQP and 60 Premier Qualifying Flights (PQF).

PQPs are generally earned based on how much a traveler spends on United-operated flights, preferred seating, upgrades, and select partner airline tickets. The requirement makes Premier 1K one of the most expensive top-tier status levels among major US airlines.

A PQP measures the money you spend on airfare and eligible credit card purchases (typically earning 1 PQP per dollar spent on base fares). A PQF counts each individual flight segment you take on United, United Express, or eligible partner airlines. PQFs include layover segments. For instance, a round trip flight with a layover in each direction equals four PQFs earned.

The qualification requirements have steadily increased throughout the loyalty program's history. Following the merger with Continental Airlines and a broader airline industry trend toward revenue-based loyalty programs, United has increasingly prioritized spending over simply logging miles flown. Today, how much a passenger spends matters significantly more than how far they travel.

According to NerdWallet, one cannot simply earn Premier 1K status simply through spending on one of United's Chase cards. While a strong supplement in the pursuit of Premier 1K, it is not enough alone to suffice. United requires a four PQF minimum in order to qualify for any premier status, including the entry level Premier Silver.

While Premier 1K may traditionally be associated with road warriors flying hundreds of thousands of miles annually, United's current rules allow members to earn the vast majority of the required 28,000 PQP through credit card spending. The absolute maximum utilizing credit card spend requires 28,000 PQP, plus the four-flight minimum. Depending on the specific Chase card in use, one can earn 1 PQP per $20 spent or 1 PQP per $15 spent, translating to $560,000 or $420,000 in credit card spend annually.

In practical terms, a traveler pursuing status exclusively through credit card spending must supplement their spending with four PQF segments on United or an authorized partner airline. Business travelers whose employers pay for frequent premium cabin trips often reach the threshold naturally, whereas leisure travelers typically require a more deliberate strategy involving credit card spending and frequent travel.

This is certainly bad news for United MileagePlus members.

United's leadership has repeatedly emphasized that Premier 1K is intended to reward the airline's most loyal and highest-value customers. While MileagePlus has evolved significantly since its 1981 launch, the core philosophy remains centered around recognizing travelers who consistently choose United throughout the year. That philosophy is reflected in the program's modern qualification structure, where spending and engagement with the airline carry greater weight than mileage alone.

Jarad Fisher, President of United MileagePlus, joined United in February, having a proven track record as the Chief of Delta Air Lines' SkyMiles program, as well as being the creator of the Apple Card. The Points Guy has reported that Fisher describes Premier 1K earning in 2026 as majority PQP based, with United credit cards bridging the gap.

United continues moving toward revenue-based loyalty metrics. In October 2026, the carrier announced that Premier Qualifying Flights (PQF) would be removed from status qualification beginning in 2027, leaving Premier Qualifying Points (PQP) as the primary path to elite status. The change reinforces United's view that Premier status, particularly Premier 1K, should primarily reward customer value and spending rather than simply the number of flights taken.

Reaching Premier 1K is not solely about upgrades and priority boarding. United's broader loyalty ecosystem includes benefits such as PlusPoints, Million Miler status, and occasional status match opportunities from other airlines, all of which can influence whether pursuing 1K is worthwhile. For some travelers, these supplemental benefits may ultimately provide more value than the status title itself.

Possibly the most significant benefit is PlusPoints. Upon reaching Premier 1K, members receive a substantial allocation of upgrade credits that can be used on eligible United and partner-operated flights. Unlike complimentary upgrades, PlusPoints give travelers greater control over when and where they attempt to move into a premium cabin. However, upgrade inventory remains capacity controlled, meaning even top-tier members may not always secure their preferred seat.

Million Miler status adds another layer of value for long-term United customers. Unlike annual status qualifications, Million Miler recognition rewards cumulative lifetime flying with the airline. However, becoming a Million Miler is solely based on miles flown on a United Aircraft, not credit card spend. Overall, travelers considering a long-term loyalty strategy may therefore view Premier 1K as only one component of a broader relationship with United, especially compared with travelers who simply leverage status matches between competing carriers.

Why you now need a United credit card to get any real value out of MileagePlus.

Of course, airline loyalty is not solely dictated by its frequent flyer program, but a range of other factors such as geography, service quality, and price. However, for regular visitors to New York, Los Angeles, or even Chicago, when multiple airlines and airports are of choice, is there a better top tier airline status to compare?

At Delta, travelers earn Diamond Medallion status exclusively through Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs), with a threshold of $28,000 MQDs during the qualification year. The airline's program is almost entirely revenue-based, allowing members to earn progress through flights, Delta Vacations purchases, and eligible credit card activity. Meanwhile, American Airlines awards its highest published tier, Executive Platinum, after earning 200,000 Loyalty Points, which can be accumulated through flights, co-branded credit card spending, shopping portals, hotel partners, and numerous non-flying activities. As a result, many loyalty experts consider American's program the easiest top-tier status to earn because it offers the greatest number of pathways that do not require extensive flying.

A traveler based near a United hub may find Premier 1K considerably more useful than an equivalent status elsewhere due simply to flight frequency and network coverage. Meanwhile, a traveler primarily flying through Atlanta may derive greater value from Delta Diamond Medallion, while someone based in Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) may prefer American Airlines Executive Platinum. In each case, the best loyalty program is often the one aligned with a passenger's most frequently used airport.

Discover the world's biggest airline loyalty programs, from United MileagePlus and Delta SkyMiles to Avios, LATAM Pass, and Flying Blue.

United Premier 1K remains one of the most prestigious airline status levels available in North America, but it is also one of the most difficult to achieve. Travelers must accumulate significant Premier Qualifying Points through flying, spending, or a combination of both while maintaining an active relationship with the airline throughout the qualification year. Premier 1K status brings travelers select privileges, such as checked baggage, United Club access, upgrades, and more.

MileagePlus's evolution illustrates a broader industry trend toward rewarding revenue contribution rather than simply distance flown. Benefits such as PlusPoints, priority services, expanded award availability, and upgrade opportunities can provide substantial value for those who travel regularly. Premier 1K status provides extra value for travelers based in or frequently visiting any of United's hubs, with the presence of native United Airlines staff, a United Club, and with mainline United service with upgrade ability.

Looking ahead, the trend toward revenue-based qualification appears unlikely to reverse. As airlines such as Delta, United, and American alike continue refining loyalty programs, travelers should expect qualification requirements and earning structures to evolve. As qualification thresholds continue to rise, Premier 1K increasingly represents not just frequent travel, but a substantial financial commitment to the airline and the broader MileagePlus ecosystem. A steady increase in the minimum threshold for Premier 1K has been defined by Thrifty Traveler as Pointsflation, keeping the bar high for frequent flyers. Only the most loyal United passengers have a shot at obtaining Premier 1K in today's earning environment.

#6173. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

#6172. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

#6171. Why The World's Largest Commercial Jet Engine Is A Threat To Other Powerplants

Falcons Spotters | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

GE Aerospace describes the GE9X as the largest and most powerful commercial aircraft engine ever built, and the specifications support the claim. A 134-inch front fan, a composite fan case, ceramic matrix composites in the hot section, and a 60:1 overall pressure ratio make it the most advanced large turbofan in production, and Guinness World Records certifies it as the most powerful commercial jet engine by test performance. None of that puts competitive pressure on anyone, because the engine has no rival to fight. GE holds the 777X exclusively, as it has held every 777 variant since the 777-200LR.

Where the engine matters commercially is on an aircraft it has never powered. Rolls-Royce has supplied the only engine ever offered on the Airbus A350, a position no competitor has challenged in two decades, and Airbus is now studying a stretched version of that aircraft aimed at the roughly 400-seat market the 777-9 currently has to itself. A stretch of that size needs more thrust than the Trent XWB-97 produces, and the GE9X sits in exactly that class. Airbus has looked at the idea. By most accounts, GE has not shown much appetite for it.

The headline dimension is the front fan, which measures 134 inches across and carries 16 fourth-generation carbon fiber composite blades inside a composite fan case. GE’s product material claims that this makes the fan larger than a Boeing 737 fuselage. Key.Aero frames the comparison more precisely, describing the engine’s overall diameter, rather than the fan alone, as greater than the fuselage diameter of the 737 family. Either way, the GE9X is the largest installation ever hung under a commercial wing.

Thrust needs the same care. Guinness World Records lists the GE9X at a maximum thrust of 134,300 pounds, achieved during an engineering test at GE’s outdoor facility in Peebles, Ohio, on November 10, 2017, breaking the 127,900 pounds the GE90-115B recorded in 2002. Guinness also lists the engine’s rated thrust as 110,000 pounds and notes that the record reflects testing conditions rather than commercial operation. For service on the 777-9, the engine is certified to 105,000 pounds. The record figure therefore describes what the architecture can produce at its limits, not what a flight crew will ever command.

Efficiency is where the design earns its reputation. GE puts the GE9X at approximately a 10:1 bypass ratio and a 60:1 overall pressure ratio, with specific fuel consumption up to 10% better than the GE90-115B. Ceramic matrix composites appear in the combustor liner and the high-pressure turbine shrouds, parts that tolerate higher temperatures with less cooling air than the metal components they replace. GE says the engine received FAA certification in September 2020, after 27,000 cycles and 17,000 hours of testing.

Every A350 ever built flies behind the same engine. Rolls-Royce supplies the Trent XWB as the family’s sole powerplant across a thrust range. Simple Flying puts it at 84,000 to 97,000 pounds, and no alternative has ever been offered to a customer. For a widebody that has sold in A350 numbers, that is unusual, and it exists because of a decision GE made rather than a competition Rolls-Royce won.

Aero-News Network reported in 2008 that GE executives had told Airbus the company would not build an engine to compete with the GE90 it supplies for the 777, leaving Airbus with a Trent variant as its only option for the A350. Airbus sales chief John Leahy had already closed the other door, saying, “We have no intention of putting their GEnx engine on the A350 at all.” GE’s view was that the GEnx suited the smaller A350 variants but could not economically scale to the thrust the A350-1000 required.

Commercially, the refusal was straightforward. GE is the exclusive engine supplier for the 777-200LR, the 777-300ER and the 777 freighter, and the A350-1000 was designed to take sales from precisely those aircraft. Developing a 97,000-pound engine for Airbus would have handed airlines a GE-powered alternative to a GE-powered Boeing, buying a share of one program at the cost of a monopoly on another. Rolls-Royce, which had lost the 777 engine competition to the GE90, took the work instead and has held the position ever since.

While around 34% of the Dreamliners flying today have RR engines, only around 8% of the known engine option orders are for RR engines.

Airbus has been circling a larger A350 for most of 2026. Commercial aircraft CEO Lars Wagner told the media in Toulouse that a decision on stretching both the A350 and the A220 would come before 2030, adding that there is “clearly” demand from the industry for longer versions of each. Aerospace Global News reported that Wagner tied both projects to viable business cases and board approval, while acknowledging that customers are waiting for each aircraft.

Thrust is the obstacle that makes the engine question unavoidable. AIN reported that a stretch would need more thrust than the A350-1000’s Trent XWB-97 can provide, and that the alternatives are limited. By AIN’s reckoning, one option would be the GE9X that powers the 777-9, an engine already certified in the class a 400-seat Airbus would require. Rolls-Royce has signaled nothing publicly about an XWB above 97,000 pounds, leaving the stretch dependent either on an unannounced derivative or on a supplier Airbus has never used on the program.

Wagner’s own answer was carefully incomplete. Pressed by reporters on whether Rolls-Royce would automatically keep its exclusive position on a prospective A350-2000, he declined to confirm it, and he declined to specify whether Airbus is engaged with GE Aerospace on supplying engines for the aircraft. He did say Airbus is happy with Rolls-Royce and that the exclusive partnership “works well” for the A350 family. Those two positions aren't contradictory, but together they fall short of the commitment Rolls-Royce has enjoyed since the program began.

The obstacle to the GE9X on an A350 is not Rolls-Royce. Reuters reported in October that industry sources say Airbus has toyed with using a GE Aerospace engine for the roughly 400-seat A350-2000, but that the engine maker has so far shown limited interest in joining. Airbus, in other words, has considered the option and GE has not pursued it.

Nothing about the underlying arithmetic has changed since 2008. GE holds the 777X exclusively, and a 400-seat A350 would compete directly against the 777-9 rather than against the aging 777-300ER. Supplying an engine for that aircraft would mean competing with a program GE already owns outright, at a moment when the 777X backlog represents years of engine deliveries and decades of aftermarket revenue. AIN noted the politics of an Airbus-GE widebody partnership as a complication in its own right, separate from the engineering.

Practical constraints sit on top of the commercial ones. The GE9X has no application outside the 777X, which means every development dollar spent adapting it for an Airbus wing would serve a single prospective customer on an aircraft that has not been launched. GE is also still closing out problems with the engine it has. AIN listed a variable guide-vane issue and, more recently, a mid-seal durability issue among the technical challenges the engine has encountered during 777-9 flight testing. An engine maker working through durability findings on its newest product is not an obvious candidate to open a second airframe program.

The Boeing 787 comes with both GE and Rolls-Royce engine options, although GE's engines have become more popular in recent times.

Volume is the real measure of the GE9X’s position. At the Dubai Airshow on November 17, 2025, Emirates ordered 65 additional 777-9s worth $38 billion at list prices, taking its total Boeing orderbook to 315 widebodies; 270 777Xs, 10 777 freighters and 35 787s. The same announcement raised the airline’s GE9X commitment to 540 engines, including 130 added that day, making Emirates the largest GE9X customer by a wide margin. Deliveries from that orderbook run through 2038.

Emirates also bought optionality that could extend the engine’s run. The carrier signed up for options to convert its latest 777-9 order into the 777-10 or the 777-8, which Emirates described as backing for Boeing’s feasibility study on the larger 777-10. Any 777-10 would use the same engine, since no alternative exists for the airframe.

Certification is what stands between the backlog and revenue. GE identified a durability problem with the GE9X mid-seal after a crack was found during a January 2026 shop visit on a 777X flight-test engine, a component chief financial officer Rahul Ghai described as “one of the parts that connects the front and the back of the engine.” Air Data News reported that the FAA will not certify the 777-9 until it approves the redesigned seal, citing an agency official speaking to FlightGlobal; GE is seeking that approval by the end of 2026, and Boeing is still targeting first delivery in 2027. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said in September that “We may see some of the testing spill into next year,” because GE had needed more testing than expected to validate the fix. Reuters has put the program six years behind schedule, with more than $15 billion in charges.

#6170. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
