It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

#6168. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

#6167. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6166. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6165. Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

If you want to learn more about the Blue Delta Amex Card, follow this link.

#6164. Too Fast? United Airlines' Starlink Rollout Is So Rapid, Some Planes Still Have Their Old WiFi Antennas

United Airlines has been steadily improving its product and customer experience to move upmarket and compete head-on with Delta Air Lines, the premium leader in the US, for years. The carrier has made genuine shifts and has been rewarded with improving financials, to the point that it now regularly posts results nearly as impressive as Delta's. One weak point, however, is that the airline's onboard WiFi systems have lagged behind what competitors offered going into the 2020s.

But in 2024, United announced that it would install Starlink WiFi across its entire mainline and regional fleets, comprising over 1,600 aircraft. It aims to complete Starlink retrofits by the end of 2027, which is an ambitious target given the sheer size of the combined fleet. To achieve this quickly, the airline is rapidly sending aircraft for retrofits, and United has placed such an emphasis on speed that it's installing Starlink on some aircraft without removing their legacy systems.

Starlink, a subsidiary of SpaceX, is a relatively new player in the inflight WiFi market. However, Starlink systems provide much faster onboard connectivity than those offered by companies such as Viasat, Thales, or Panasonic, and the company even formerly mandated that airline customers offer it to passengers for free (this is reportedly no longer the case). As such, it's become extremely popular with passengers, while airlines have been lining up for the service.

United announced Starlink in September 2024, with the roll-out beginning in 2025. It later announced that it aimed to have all mainline and regional aircraft equipped with Starlink by the end of 2027, which meant an extremely rapid roll-out given the sheer size of the fleet. Initially, United focused on retrofitting Starlink onto the United Express fleet, as the service contract for the providers on this fleet was set to end shortly. Soon afterward, Starlink started coming to mainline.

The official United Starlink tracker shows that all Bombardier CRJ550s and Embraer E175s have been completed. 346 narrowbody aircraft have been retrofitted, and United has installed Starlink on the Airbus A321neo, A321XLR, Boeing 737-800, 737-900ER, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 9. In addition, United has now installed Starlink on four 777-200ERs, one 777-300ER, and two 787-8s. Overall, about 46% of the fleet is retrofitted: 705 aircraft out of the 1,632 aircraft flying for United and United Express.

Earlier this month, a United 737-900ER was spotted parked at a gate and shared on X with two Starlink antennas (United's standard configuration for the system) and its older Viasat antenna. Similarly, a 737-900 was also spotted, equipped with Starlink and Viasat antennas, according to an X post.

One advertised benefit of Starlink is quick installation, but it appears the main holdup in the retrofit project is the time required to remove the aircraft's previous WiFi equipment. On some aircraft, the airline simply left it on for now to speed up the process.

United has just over a year remaining until its end-of-2027 deadline, and only 46% of the fleet is completed. There's a high chance that this timeline could slip, but Starlink is meant to be a major commercial advantage for the airline. A clean Starlink installation is advertised as taking as little as eight hours, which is significantly faster than installation times for other WiFi systems. However, the full retrofit also requires removing the previous WiFi system, which can add significantly more time.

United states that its full timeline, including removing the legacy system, is about three to four days. To get the entire fleet retrofitted by the end of 2027, it would need to have a significant number of aircraft out of service, which is lost revenue. Therefore, the carrier has decided to shorten the timeline for N78438 and N37409 by leaving the Viasat system on for the time being, and it remains to be seen whether it will continue this practice in the future.

Starlink WiFi Tracker means you always know what connectivity you will have on a United Airlines flight.

Starlink is now flying on United's Bombardier and Embraer aircraft, along with the A321neo, 737, 777, and 787. However, it still operates a substantial number of aircraft with older WiFi systems. All the non-Starlink widebodies are equipped with Panasonic systems, while the narrowbody fleet features a mix of Panasonic, Viasat, and Thales systems. While Starlink is offered for free, the other systems generally require payment upfront, and none of the three offers the same speeds as Starlink.

American Airlines generally offers Viasat WiFi on its domestic fleet, which is complimentary for AAdvantage members, while most of the widebodies are equipped with Panasonic systems. Delta offers either Viasat or Hughes WiFi on nearly its entire fleet. The benefit is that Viasat and Hughes offer much faster speeds than Panasonic and Thales. The downside for these airlines is that Starlink offers even faster speeds. But for United, it's now offering the fastest and slowest WiFi systems among its rivals.

United is banking on Starlink becoming a major commercial advantage over its rivals, but it will only be a true advantage once the system is available across United's entire fleet. A better WiFi system on its own is not necessarily a reason for customers to choose one airline over the other, but it's becoming an increasingly important factor in purchasing decisions. As United continues to aim for product and a premium brand, Starlink is becoming increasingly important to the airline's selling proposition.

By moving upmarket and becoming a 'premium' airline brand, United is hoping to be a carrier that wins customers' business based on its name and product. This is the strategy that Delta first implemented under CEO Richard Anderson after its 2008 merger with Northwest Airlines, and Delta is now the most successful airline in the country. But of course, the US carriers don't make their money by selling flight tickets; rather, the money is in loyalty programs.

United offers Starlink for free, but it's only accessible with a MileagePlus account number. A customer who signs up for MileagePlus and accesses Starlink may be more inclined to fly with United in the future. From there, they may be more likely to sign up for a MileagePlus co-branded credit card, which is where the real money is. United and its contemporaries sell huge amounts of miles to their credit card partners at little cost, and it's in the airlines' best interests to increase demand for these miles.

United has been tremendously successful in pursuing this strategy, and Starlink is meant to be a crucial advantage. United CEO Scott Kirby has publicly said Starlink is a major selling point for the airline and that the carrier waited until competitors committed to systems like those offered by Viasat to gain an edge. Of course, while Starlink is a major competitive advantage for United, this won't necessarily be true across the US.

United's new network upgrades take a big step forward.

American Airlines announced in May that it would install Starlink across its entire Airbus fleet, consisting of the A319-100, A320-200, A321-200, and A321neo, to begin in 2027. Last month, however, the carrier announced that it would expand the Starlink program to all mainline aircraft. The carrier has not stated that Starlink will come to the American Eagle fleet, but it will significantly elevate American's overall product offering as it also tries to move upmarket and become a premium brand.

Delta, on the other hand, has not signed a deal with Starlink at all. Instead, Delta has committed to installing Amazon's upcoming Leo system on approximately half of its fleet. Reportedly, Delta and Starlink experienced conflicts about integrating the system into Delta's existing 'Delta Sync' portal, while there may have also been a personal conflict with Starlink CEO Elon Musk. However, the actual decision to go with Amazon would undoubtedly have been made after considering multiple factors as part of a larger commercial deal.

The issue for Delta is that Amazon Leo is not in service yet. The airline plans to begin installing Leo in 2028, when United is supposed to have already completed its Starlink retrofit. While the Viasat and Hughes systems Delta already offers are competent and free, Starlink offers faster speeds, and United has now established itself as the leader in the US airline industry, whereas Delta used to be. Considering how brand-conscious Delta is, this is not an enviable position.

#6163. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6162. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

#6161. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6160. Chase Ink Business Preferred Card Bonus: 100K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card has a phenomenal sign-up bonus of 100,000 points after spending $8,000 within three first three months, and there’s lots of value to this card in the long term, especially thanks to its reasonable $95 annual fee — read my Ink Preferred review here. If you’re eligible for the card, there’s no reason not to apply.

This is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and it’s arguably Chase’s most rewarding and best value business credit card. In this post I’d like to go over the Ink Business Preferred bonus details, including eligibility requirements.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card with 100K bonus points

The Chase Ink Preferred Card currently has a welcome offer of 100,000 Ultimate Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

#6158. Why The GCAP Is The Only 6th-Generation Fighter Jet The Rest Of The World Can Actually Buy

In June 2026, Germany announced it was withdrawing from the FCAS 6th-generation fighter jet project with France and Spain. This left the GCAP/Tempest as the only credible European-led sixth-generation fighter jet program. The GCAP intends to be a reasonably heavy sixth-generation air superiority fighter jet built with an emphasis on multirole missions.

It is also being designed explicitly with an eye to exports. Developing a true sixth-generation fighter jet that functions as part of a fully integrated networked kill chain is now so complicated and so expensive that it can strain any nation's aerospace industry to the breaking point (with the possible exceptions of the US and China).

Even so, there is discussion in Washington over whether the US aerospace industry has the bandwidth to develop two next-generation fighters side by side. Some advocate delaying the F/A-XX until after the F-47 is more developed.

Fighter jet purchases are high-profile political affairs that can become politically heated quickly. This is often seen in South America and now in Canada, on the topic of purchasing US fighter jets (vs Swedish Gripens). Many countries do not wish to purchase US fighter jets for geopolitical reasons.

Indonesia is an extreme example of a country exploring purchasing fighter jets from half a dozen countries to ensure no country has too much control over its fighter jet fleet (through spare parts and software updates). It has indicated that Turkish KAAN fighters would need to be free from US ITAR restrictions, a very tall ask.

A range of factors, from Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 to the passage of CAASTA in 2017 to the sanctions of 2022, have contributed to Russia's fighter jet export market collapsing. It has become infeasible for dozens of countries, including all NATO member Eastern European countries, to purchase Russian fighters.

Indeed, Serbia said it was infeasible to purchase Russian fighters and so opted for French Rafales. Elsewhere, China is emerging on the stage as a serious export market for higher-end fighter jets. However, while some countries like Egypt, the UAE, and Argentina have openly touted purchasing Chinese fighters, only Pakistan has done so (J-10Cs and possibly upcoming J-35s).

Many African countries and others have purchased lower-end Chinese fighters or advanced trainers. For many countries, purchasing Chinese fighters remains geopolitically complicated and is out of the question for non-aligned countries like Vietnam and India.

Being developed by the UK, Italy, and Japan, the GCAP offers an alternative to the US, China, and Russia that can be more geopolitically salient for many countries. This is somewhat similar to how Canadians are currently viewing the Saab Gripen. It's not an 'enemy' Chinese or Russian fighter, but it's not fully American either.

Australia, Saudi Arabia, and India have expressed interest in GCAPand the collapse of FCAS has reduced their options. It has also opened the door to the possibility of Germany (and possibly Spain) joining the program in some capacity. It would be a major boon for the GCAP if Germany were to join, as the trio (and particularly the UK) is currently struggling with financing the ambitious program by itself.

Another important aspect is that any country can market its fighter jet as whatever generation they like. Pakistan has promoted later JF-17 variants, particularly the Block III, as possessing capabilities associated with 4.5-generation fighters (sometimes 4.5 'plus'). Sukhoi's marketing suggested its proposed Su-75 Checkmate low-cost fighter would be a fifth-generation fighter rivaling the F-35.

Fighter jet generation labels are part marketing, part clickbait, and part useful. The engineering of a next-generation aircraft is less about visible features (such as tailless vs large vertical stabilizers) and more about internal features (thermal management, sensor fusion, and networking).

Without Germany, serious analysts do not think France will have the capacity to develop a fully-fledged sixth-generation fighter jet alone. France's Dassault has said it plans to go it alone and develop a next-generation fighter, although analysts expect this to be a lighter-weight, less ambitious carrier-based aircraft and closer to something like a fifth-generation 'plus' fighter.

Perhaps a more important question is what Germany will do. Germany could partner with Sweden (and/or Spain) and develop a sixth-generation fighter jet that could compete with the GCAP. Even if it does, the GCAP has a head start, although such a jet could compete with GCAP sometime in the 2040s.

Prototype/demonstrator flying, three-engined

Germany could throw its weight behind the GCAP, or another option could be for it to purchase more F-35s and focus on developing advanced teaming combat drones. Other programs, like South Korea's KF-21 and Turkey's KAAN fighter jet, are 4.5-generation fighter jets with low-observable characteristics.

These countries have plans to introduce later block upgrades to make them closer to fifth-generation jets. But they are not likely to compete in the GCAP's segment directly. Sweden could theoretically go it alone and develop a next-generation successor to the Saab Gripen, but it would likely be much less ambitious than the GCAP.

For now, the primary advanced frontline fighter jet the US offers on the export market is the F-35. In practice, in the late 2030s and 2040s, it could be a future F-35 Block 5 that will be the primary export competitor to the GCAP, although this is somewhat speculative. A future F-35 Block 5 could be a fifth-generation 'plus' fighter or thought of as a fifth-generation fighter with sixth-generation characteristics.

The primary 6th-generation jet the US is developing is the F-47. This is intended as the tip of the spear air dominance fighter. Its niche role is seen in how few the Air Force states it wants to purchase (185+), around a tenth of its program of record for the F-35A. The F-47 is designed to replace the F-22 and complement the F-35.

Importantly, it is designed for USAF requirements without much regard for export air force requirements (unlike the GCAP and the F-35). In March 2025, US President Donald Trump said a downgraded version of the F-47 would be available for export, although this is not his Administration's decision to make.

It is the decision of later administrations. The export ban on the F-22 provides precedent for a future export ban. Even less is known about the Navy's F/A-XX, and it is possible land-based variants could be attractive on the export market (like the Hornet/Super Hornet were), but again, this is speculative.

As stated, many countries have geopolitical issues with purchasing Chinese and Russian fighters. But there are other issues. One is that China has imposed an export ban on its high-end J-20 Mighty Dragon, much like the US and its F-22. This offers a precedent that China might be reluctant to export its leading next-generation fighter (possibly the J-36), but may be willing to export lower-level jets (such as the J-50).

The US and China are the only two countries large enough to comfortably develop sixth-generation fighter jets exclusively for their own needs. Other countries like Russia, Japan, the UK, and France are forced to partner with other countries to spread the burden and/or design the aircraft for export in mind.

As a rule, export jets need to be multirole, and able to fill many missions for smaller air forces. The French 'omnirole' Rafale is a great example. For Russia, there is another issue. It doesn't appear to have a credible sixth-generation fighter program. The last major update from Rostec on the MiG-41/PAK DP (often termed a fifth-generation 'plus' interceptor) was in 2021.

There is also no evidence that the program is a fully funded program with full state backing and commitment. Instead, it appears Russia is focusing on producing its mature Su-30/34/35 series, developing russified commercial aircraft, and maturing its Su-57 Felon.

Additive manufacturing is being used to build Rolls-Royce turbofans.

For now, it seems the GCAP/Tempest is the world's only credible, fully-funded sixth-generation program designed as a multirole platform useful to a range of air forces. The US F-47 appears highly niche, and the US's willingness to export the jet remains questionable. Before the US banned the highly specialized F-22, Japan, Israel, and Australia were considered three of the very few potential customers.

The GCAP remains the most ambitious next-generation program for the export market with committed funding. The first demonstrator is now being built by BAE Systems and is expected to fly in 2027. Japan remains adamant that it wants the jet to be in service by 2035, which would easily make it the first non-US and non-Chinese sixth-generation fighter to enter service.

#6156. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.

What do you make of these World of Hyatt changes?

(again, ick on that last statement).

#6155. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

In January 2026, Lufthansa formally announced plans to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks…

Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and currently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its new Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”

With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

In recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

Lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the new Allegris seats up there.

For once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the new Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a new business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

Rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

Lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s new A380 business class?

#6154. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6153. Amex Gold Card Credits: How To Maximize $424 In Uber, Dining, Resy, & Dunkin’ Value

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the best cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it also has an excellent welcome offer. The card is ideal for anyone who spends a lot on dining, whether at restaurants or supermarkets, and in my experience, getting approved for the card is quite easy.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), though the card also offers up to $424 in annual credits, which could more than offset the annual fee, not even accounting for all the other perks.

Now, a vast majority of cardmembers aren’t going to maximize all the Amex Gold Card credits, since it is a bit of a “coupon book” vibe, in terms of how the credits are issued. In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Amex Gold Card credits, including the restrictions, and how they can be redeemed.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

With the Amex Gold Card credits, cardmembers can potentially receive statement credits with Uber, select dining establishments, Resy, and Dunkin’. The terms associated with using each of these Amex Gold credits varies, so it’s worth covering all the details. Below is a chart with the basics, and then I’ll cover all the credits in more detail. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit? As someone who uses both Uber and Uber Eats more than once per month, the Amex Gold Uber Cash credit benefit is basically as good as cash to me. Obviously if you don’t use Uber or Uber Eats that often, try to remember to use it earlier in the month, so you don’t forget to use it later on. That’s especially true if you have international travel plans, given that the credit only works in the United States.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in dining credits annually:

What’s my take on the Amex Gold dining credit? Everyone has different spending patterns. Personally, I don’t frequently dine at any of the establishments included with the Amex Gold dining credit, though I do use Grubhub once in a while. So when I can remember to use the perk, that saves me $10 per month on those purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

Let me emphasize that you don’t have to jump through hoops at a restaurant to take advantage of the Amex Gold Resy statement credit. You don’t even have to make your reservation through Resy, as long as it’s a Resy partner restaurant.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Resy credit? If you dine out frequently and live in a decently sized city, visiting a Resy restaurant should be super easy. Personally, I’m able to maximize this without even trying, since I go to restaurants associated with Resy all the time.

Admittedly, this is of limited use to those in small towns, where not many restaurants may use the Resy platform. In those situations, remember to consider Resy restaurants when you’re traveling to a larger city, as that’s your best bet for maximizing that perk.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

You can maximize the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit by spending at least $7 per month at a Dunkin’ location with your eligible card.

What’s my take on the Amex Gold Dunkin’ credit? Admittedly, this is niche, and seems like an odd fit for a premium card. Dunkin’ isn’t exactly a high-end brand, and the $7 credit seems quite random. However, I think this is easy enough to manage. It’s also worth emphasizing that as of now, simply loading your Dunkin’ account through the Dunkin’ app with $7 per month seems to trigger the credit.

Based on how I read the terms, that’s not even a fluke. The terms say the credit can’t be used for gift cards, though loading a Dunkin’ account isn’t a gift card. So as things currently stand, basically view this as an $84 annual Dunkin’ credit (which you must load monthly, but the credit as such won’t expire).

Just about any card with perks that are distributed throughout the year and where enrollment is required will have a significant amount of breakage. That’s only natural, and as I see it, it’s a double-edged sword. On the plus side, I view it as an opportunity for savvy consumers to get outsized value from a card. At the same time, “credit card fatigue” is a very real concept.

With that in mind, how much do I value the up to $424 in credits offered on the Amex Gold Card? Here’s my general thought process:

When all is said and done, I’d say that I value the credits on the Amex Gold Card as maybe being within $100 of the card’s annual fee, give or take. To me, that essentially puts this Membership Rewards points-earning powerhouse in line with other mid-range cards, in terms of the cost of holding onto it. Everyone’s math will differ, so crunch the numbers to decide how much value the card offers to you.

The Amex Gold Card is a product you primarily get for the excellent return it offers on everyday spending. The card has a steep annual fee, though the good news is that this can largely be offset thanks to the up to $424 in annual credits it offers. Hopefully, the above is a useful rundown of how each of the Amex Gold Card credits can be used.

The Amex Gold credits won’t be equally valuable for everyone, but if you dine at Resy restaurants and use Uber (for rides or food delivery) with any frequency, you should be able to recoup much of the annual fee thanks to the credits.

What do you make of the Amex Gold Card credits, and how much value are you able to get out of them?
