Cruises can be truly affordable vacations — but that doesn’t mean you won’t run up a significant bill booking your sailing or spending during your trip. It’s also easy to overspend on certain travel costs when you don’t know all the best money-saving tricks.

As someone who cruises often, I don’t have a huge budget to spend on onboard purchases for each sailing, so I’ve had to get wise on how to save money on a cruise.

Some of my strategies are obvious and others I’ve learned from trial and error over more than 80 sailings. I’m happy to share the wealth, so to speak, so you can avoid money mistakes and stretch your travel budget as far as it can possibly go. Here are my 35 top tips on how to save on a cruise.

Book early. Most cruise lines increase prices as ships sell out. Book early to get the lowest prices, as well as the widest choice of cabin types and locations, plus dining times.

Book at the last minute. The corollary advice is that cruise lines will sometimes drop prices or offer value-added promotions on cruises that have too many available cabins left a few months before their scheduled departures. You can find cheap deals on last-minute sailings, especially if you’re not picky about which cabin you get. Start looking about 90 days out for most big-ship sailings.

Related: When is the best time to book a cruise?

Book a shoulder-season sailing. Spring and fall tend to be less busy travel times, and cruises during these shoulder-season months are priced accordingly. Pick a cruise at the beginning or end of the Alaska or Mediterranean season when the weather isn’t as optimal, and you’ll save big over the peak midseason voyages. Sailings departing after Thanksgiving but before Christmas are also less popular and, therefore, cheaper.

Book an inside cabin. The cheapest room on the ship is an inside cabin, so choose one of those rooms if you want to spend less on your next sailing. You’ll get access to the same pools, restaurants, shows and activities as the folks in the balcony cabins; all you’re missing out on is a window and some more floor space. Some people actually prefer inside cabins for amazing sleep in the pitch dark or because they spend all their time out and about on the ship and are never in their room.

Be flexible on dates. Many unpredictable factors combine to make one sailing more expensive than the identical itinerary the week before or after. If you can be flexible on which week you cruise, you can save money by choosing whichever sail date is cheaper.

Book an older ship. Newer ships with their one-of-a-kind attractions and up-to-date everything get all the attention — and can command the highest prices. Seek out older ships to get a better cruise deal. Cruise lines maintain their older ships and often give them massive makeovers to add the latest restaurants and top-deck attractions, so you’ll hardly notice you’re on a 20-year-old ship. But your budget will notice the more affordable rates, leaving money in your pocket to spend on splurges like spa treatments and specialty dining.

Look for sales and promotions. Cruise lines run sales so often that you’re wasting money if you book when there isn’t a deal. Some promotions are all about lower fares, while others save you money with included perks, like free Wi-Fi or a complimentary beverage package. Solo travelers should look out for sales that waive the single supplement, saving you up to 50% of the normal single cabin price. Families should watch out for kids-cruise-free sales or other discounted third- and fourth-guest offers.

How do you find out about your favorite cruise line’s latest sales? Sign up for the brand’s email list or a large online travel agent’s deal alert newsletter, and they’ll send info on promos straight to your inbox.

Check for price drops. If you book a cruise and discover that the price has decreased down the road, your cruise line or travel agent will often be able to issue you a price adjustment. Some passengers have even reported receiving more than one adjustment if the prices fall repeatedly. The key is to make sure you spot the lower prices before the final payment deadline passes. After that, the best a cruise line can usually do for your is to offer a cabin upgrade.

Related: The best cruise booking perks — and which ones are actually free

Leverage your casino play. Cruise lines love casino players because they spend money on board. Once you’ve established yourself as a member of a cruise line’s players club, you might find yourself the recipient of cruise discounts and complimentary casino cruise offers. You can definitely save on a cruise when all you have to pay are taxes and fees.

Be loyal to one cruise line. Sail once with a cruise line, and you’re eligible to join its loyalty program. All members are eligible for select past-passenger cruise fare discounts, but the most loyal members can access free upgrades or even free cruises.

Request your shareholder credit. Cruisers who own 100 shares or more of the big three publicly traded cruise corporations — Carnival Corp., Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings and Royal Caribbean Group — can request onboard credit as a perk of being a shareholder. You can request it via an online form on each cruise line's website; the amount you'll receive, if approved, depends on the type of cruise you book. Credit can only be requested on full-fare voyages, and only one shareholder credit is permitted per stateroom.

Choose a drive-to port. Parking a car for a week is almost guaranteed to be cheaper than airport transfers, flights and a precruise hotel for a family of four. Cruise ships depart from ports all along the U.S. and Canada coastlines; consider choosing a cruise that departs from a port within driving distance of your home to save money on your next cruise.

Use a credit card that gives you perks. Even if your cruise fare isn't dirt cheap, you can still get more value from your vacation dollars when you pay for that vacation at sea with the right card. For example, book with The Platinum Card® from American Express, and its Cruise Privileges Program will get you double Membership Rewards points, onboard credit and cruise line-specific perks. Book a Carnival cruise with the Carnival Rewards™ Mastercard®, and you can earn extra Carnival Rewards points that you can redeem for cruise-related purchases and Loyalty Status stars that will fast track your elite status.

Or, perhaps you can use your cruise final payment to make the minimum spending requirement on a new credit card and get a slew of points or miles you can use for a free trip down the road.

Related: Should you get a cruise line credit card? Here’s a closer look

Bid for an upgrade. Several major cruise lines, like Norwegian Cruise Line and MSC Cruises, offer select guests the option to bid for an upgraded cabin. Bid less than the difference between your cabin cost and the price of the nicer room, and if your bid is approved, you’ll get upgraded onboard digs at a discount.

Use a travel agent. Most travel agents won’t charge you to use their cruise-booking services, but they can help you find the best deal on the best sailing for you, and they might even throw in a free bottle of Champagne or some onboard credit. If nothing else, these knowledgeable advisers can save you from making costly mistakes on the wrong cruise purchases, and that is a value in and of itself.

Book your next cruise on board. Most cruise lines run a future cruise sales desk on board ships. If you put a deposit down on a future cruise while sailing on the current one, you can be eligible for discounts and onboard credit (i.e., free spending money for you).

Related: Mistakes to avoid when booking your cruise

Get first-day discounts. Embarkation day can be chaotic. You’re getting familiar with the ship’s layout, signing up for all the things and likely going to the main dining room for dinner to meet your waiters. You might not even realize that the spa and specialty restaurants are open that evening. To lure passengers through their doors, onboard spas might offer first-day discounts and specialty restaurants might throw in a free bottle of wine.

Book activities and packages in advance. Many cruise lines offer discounts for booking drink packages, Wi-Fi plans and shore excursions online before your cruise. It will save you money on your next cruise if you do some precruise planning instead of being spontaneous once on board.

Go to the spa on port days. Most passengers get off the ship when it’s docked in port, so they prefer to book spa treatments on sea days. (The salon is especially busy on formal nights.) Cruise ship spas will often run specials or discounts to entice passengers to book treatments on port days, saving you money on the pricey massages and body treatments.

Enjoy specialty restaurants at lunch. You can rack up quite the cruise bill dining at specialty restaurants each night of your cruise. To save money, look for extra-charge eateries that are open for lunch. The food is usually just as good, but the menu is smaller, and the prices are reduced from the dinnertime fee.

Look for daily or happy hour drink specials. Your ship’s daily activity schedule (found in a printed newsletter or the cruise line's app) is your guide to saving money. Look for daily drink specials or happy hour deals that will save you money on those tropical drinks that are the hallmark of a Caribbean vacation. Or ask at your favorite onboard bar if they ever run drink deals, and plan your visits around those times.

Book a drink or dinner package. If eating and drinking are how you spend your money on a cruise, you could save by bundling your purchases. Look for all-you-can-drink packages that will save you money if you plan to drink a lot each day or specialty dining packages that offer a discounted total price for booking multiple reservations in advance.

Know when to skip the drink package. If you’re a casual drinker who doesn’t order more than a few drinks a day (including coffee and soda), or you don’t think you can drink enough to break even on the beverage package price every day, you will save more by skipping the package and ordering drinks a la carte, especially if you can utilize happy hour specials or loyalty perks to cut costs.

Also note that NCL’s Unlimited Open Bar package that’s part of its Free at Sea booking promotion is not a truly complimentary perk; you’ll need to pay $28.50 to $32 per person, per day. If you typically don’t spend that much on cruise drinks, you’ll save more by going a la carte.

Related: Are cruise line drink packages worth the price? What to know before you buy

Skip the souvenir glass. Step onto a cruise ship pool deck or atrium on the first day of your cruise, and you’re likely to be approached by a waiter offering you a drink in a souvenir glass. You want the cocktail, but do you really need to bring home a cup shaped like Carnival’s funnel? Say yes to the drink and no to the souvenir glass, and you will save a few bucks on the cost of the drink (not to mention the extra bag fees when you realize you can’t carry all those souvenirs home).

Seek out free alcohol. If you pay attention, you can find several opportunities to get drinks for free on a cruise ship. Many of the onboard art auctions pass out Champagne or sparkling wine to attendees, and sometimes the ship’s shops will offer liquor tastings in an attempt to convince you to buy a bottle. If you’re a suite guest or loyalty member, you might be eligible for free drink vouchers, happy hours or events with comped drinks.

Shop the sales for souvenirs. Cruise line boutiques often run BOGO sales or “everything for $10” hours on items like T-shirts, evening purses and sunglasses. If you’re thinking of purchasing some souvenirs, look for promotional events listed in your daily schedule. If you want to splurge on high-end jewelry or other expensive gifts, wait for those onboard shops to announce specials. These purchases won’t be cheap, but you might be able to save a bit or get an extra bauble thrown in for free.

Check out the seminars. Your cruise ship’s spa or boutiques will often host seminars about wellness practices or understanding gemstones. These events are really marketing ploys to get you to sign up for spa treatments or buy shoe insoles or jewelry. However, they often convince people to attend by giving away spa credit or jewelry in a raffle. If you’ve got nothing better to do on a sea day, you might show up in the hopes of winning something. Spa tours and port shopping lectures also run raffles (plus, you might get a free massage for a minute).

Look for midcruise specials. Cruise ships will discount paid attractions on the fly if they need to drum up more revenue in a certain area or if restaurants are not full. If you keep your schedule flexible, you can jump on midcruise specials, advertised in your daily schedule, and save on specialty dining, arcade games, spa treatments and more.

Evaluate laundry costs. Doing laundry on board is a smart way to avoid checked bag fees by packing light. In some cases, sending a bag of laundry to be washed on board (especially if you take advantage of a midcruise laundry special) can be more economical than paying to check a bag. However, you can save even more if you take advantage of a ship’s self-serve launderette or hand wash small items in your cabin’s bathroom sink. Some top suites come with free or discounted laundry, and top-tier frequent cruisers might also get comped laundry as a loyalty perk, so check the options before packing as part of your savings strategy.

Book your own tours. Cruise lines mark up shore excursions because they have to pay the provider and turn a profit. You can often save money by going to the source and booking a tour directly with a provider. Alternatively, a private tour guide for a group might not always save you money, but you will usually get more value out of a small-group tour that you can customize to your preference.

Skip the tour and explore independently. You don’t need to shell out big bucks for an organized tour in every port. To keep costs down, skip the beach break tour and walk or take a bus or taxi to the beach. Do your own walking tour with a guidebook or app. Go on a hike or take yourself to a cathedral or museum. If you tour independently, you won’t have to pay for a guide or cruise line overhead.

Look for less inclusive beach breaks. Sometimes a cruise line will offer several versions of the same resort day pass or beach break excursion — one that just covers your entrance and another that includes lunch and drinks and water toy use. If you don’t plan to eat or drink that much, or at all, you can save by booking the least expensive version of the tour and just paying for the amenities you use a la carte.

Use local transportation. Taxi rides can add up quickly. Consider using less expensive forms of transportation to explore a city during your port stop. Local buses and subways can be more affordable ways to get around, plus offer a glimpse into local life.

Use Wi-Fi in port. Cruise ship internet access is pricey; you might pay more for a week on board than you do for a month at home! If you don’t have to be connected at all hours, skip the cruise ship Wi-Fi plan and seek out free or cheap Wi-Fi in port. Many port terminals have free Wi-Fi, or you can grab a cup of coffee or a drink at an establishment in town with complimentary Wi-Fi for customers.

Negotiate prices. Know when prices aren’t set in stone and negotiate a lower fee to save on your in-port purchases. You can often barter over the price of crafts, food or souvenirs in open-air markets, or negotiate rates for taxi tours or rides. Always be friendly and polite when haggling, and be prepared to walk if the vendor does not accept your offer.

Bring your own beach gear. Most beaches you’ll visit on a cruise, including the cruise lines’ private islands, will rent you snorkel gear, umbrellas and beach floats, or sell you beach toys. Save money by purchasing and bringing your own snorkel gear, beach shade, inflatable beach toys and floats. The upfront cost might be higher than a single rental, but you can use the gear in multiple ports and on multiple cruises. Look for inflatables or collapsible gear that can pack down small or come in convenient carrying cases.

Don’t eat lunch or dinner in port. I always recommend trying the local cuisine in port, both because it’s a fun way to experience a new culture and to support the local economy. But if you’re on a budget and need to cut costs, skip the meals in port and head back to the ship for meals in the many included eateries on board. Don’t forget to fill up on breakfast, so you can spend more time in port before hunger drives you back to the ship.

If nothing else, avoid the overpriced and often inauthentic waterside tourist restaurants and ask around for where locals eat on the cheap — or skip the lunch and treat yourself to a cheaper gelato or pastry instead.

You don’t have to employ every one of these tips to save money on your next sailing, but keep them in mind to make smart decisions as you plan your next vacation and once you’re on board. It’s always OK to splurge a little on vacation, but you want to make sure you’re not spending unnecessarily. What matters is that you’re getting the biggest benefit from your vacation buck.

#6108. The FAA Still Uses Floppy Disks In Air Traffic Control—And Hopes To Replace Them In 2028 [Roundup]

News and notes from around the interweb: FAA expects to finally retire floppy disks for air traffic control by 2028 The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) announced…that it has begun phasing out floppy disks used in air traffic control operations. …The first five facilities receiving the upgrades include Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport, as well as data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The FAA says it plans to install E-IDSs at 435 sites by the end of 2028.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) announced…that it has begun phasing out floppy disks used in air traffic control operations. …The first five facilities receiving the upgrades include Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport, as well as data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. #6107. Lufthansa Announced Columbus, Ohio Flight—Then City Council Blocked Part Of The Subsidy

Lufthansa announced Columbus’ first scheduled nonstop flight to Europe last month. Now the city council has refused to approve the first $300,000 of the mayor’s promised support for it. The Frankfurt flights are still scheduled to start May 5, 2027. But the fight exposes something that tends to get lost in the celebration of a new international route: local officials helped make the numbers work by offering up taxpayer money to protect the airline if route revenue falls short, and the city’s portion still needed council approval. Lufthansa plans to fly Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays using a Boeing 787-9 with Allegris business class. There’ll be 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 coach seats. The region has 38 German companies, Bayer is building a pharmaceutical plant in New Albany, and Frankfurt offers connections throughout Europe and beyond. With the city using residents’ money to guarantee it, Lufthansa’s downside is protected trying it out. The revenue guarantee draws support from several sources: Contributor Reported Support City of Columbus Up to $1 million over three years. Council blocked the proposed first $300,000 installment. Franklin County Up to $1 million over three years. JobsOhio Participating, with the amount not publicly confirmed. Councilmember Rob Dorans says his briefing identified $1 million. Columbus Partnership and local businesses Financial support promised, with the amount undisclosed. Lufthansa would collect under the guarantee if revenue falls below the agreed target, subject to caps and a three year limit. The airport’s current incentive program also offers Frankfurt service $1 million in marketing support over two years, plus two years of landing fee, terminal rent and international inspection fee waivers. That’s available as long as they operate at least 100 departures annually over at least six months. The city’s $300,000 was included in a proposed $1 million grant to One Columbus, the regional economic development organization. On November 16, council unanimously removed the airline money and subsequently approved the remaining $700,000. Dorans objects both to the spending priority and to how the deal was handled. He says residents needing help should come first, and accuses the administration of negotiating without council involvement. The administration says all nine councilmembers were offered briefings and eight participated, including Dorans. Meanwhile, Council President Shannon Hardin is running for mayor against the incumbent whose administration owns this deal. And the councilmember who introduced the amendment pulling funding actually supports the funding. That was a maneuver that allows him to bring the funding back for another vote. You’d expect Lufthansa to have an agreement spelling out its revenue guarantee before announcing the flight. Oops. It appears not every organization contributing money already made a firm commitment. The city ordinance was seeking authority to enter into a grant agreement with One Columbus. The council wasn’t technically voting to cancel a Lufthansa contract, just on whether to appropriate the funds to the entity that had promised Lufthansa a fixed guarantee. The Columbus Partnership says it still expects the flight to happen. Council could reconsider, or other backers could fill the funding gap. I’ve covered this sort of bidding for service before, including Austin offering incentives for international flights and Pittsburgh subsidizing Qatar Airways cargo service. Usually these subsidies either go to flights that would have made money anyway, or get burned through and the flight goes away. Meanwhile, I’m betting that the money comes back. #6106. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card is a solid option for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

And with two welcome offers available, prospective cardholders have a choice to make.

The standard VentureOne currently offers 20,000 bonus miles, earned after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Meanwhile, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card - Miles Boost has a new offer: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The other key difference is the introductory APR. The standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers (followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74%; a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version, on the other hand, doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period.

Here's a closer look at both offers and how to decide which one makes the most sense for you.

There are currently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne:

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, the standard VentureOne Rewards offer is worth $370, while the VentureOne Rewards - Miles Boost offer is worth $740.

That's an additional $370 in potential value with the Miles Boost offer, provided you can meet the higher spending requirement and maximize your miles through Capital One's transfer partners.

Alternatively, you can redeem Capital One miles at a fixed rate of 1 cent apiece to cover eligible travel purchases. That would make the standard 20,000-mile offer worth $200 and the 40,000-mile Miles Boost offer worth $400.

Of course, the larger welcome bonus isn't the only factor worth considering. Here's how to decide which version of the VentureOne is right for you.

Related: The easy route: How to redeem Capital One miles at a fixed value

The biggest difference between the two VentureOne offers comes down to whether you value a larger welcome bonus or an introductory APR period.

If your goal is to maximize travel rewards and you can comfortably meet the $1,000 spending requirement, the VentureOne - Miles Boost is likely the better choice. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles as the standard VentureOne after meeting the higher spending requirement.

However, this version doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period, making it a better fit for those who plan to pay their balance in full each month — something I'd recommend regardless of which card you choose.

On the other hand, the standard VentureOne Rewards may make more sense if you're planning a large purchase and want extra time to pay it off. It offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). You'll earn fewer bonus miles, but you'll just need to spend just $500 to earn the welcome bonus.

Ultimately, both versions offer the same ongoing rewards and benefits, so the right choice depends on your financial priorities.

Related: This month's best credit card welcome bonuses

Regardless of which welcome offer you choose, both versions of the VentureOne have the same ongoing rewards structure.

That means if you meet the minimum spending requirement entirely through purchases earning the base rate, you'll earn at least 20,625 miles with the standard VentureOne or 41,250 miles with the VentureOne - Miles Boost, including the respective welcome bonuses.

One of the VentureOne's biggest selling points is that it provides access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners without an annual fee.

Both versions of the card also have no foreign transaction fees, making them useful options for international travel.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Before applying for either VentureOne offer, you'll want to understand Capital One's application restrictions.

Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. According to the issuer's current terms, you aren't eligible for a new VentureOne bonus if you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months.

Capital One may also consider other factors when reviewing your application, so approval isn't guaranteed even if you meet the bonus eligibility requirements.

Be sure to review the terms of the specific offer you're considering before applying.

Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions

The two versions of the VentureOne give prospective cardholders a choice between earning more miles upfront and taking advantage of an introductory APR period.

For travelers who can comfortably meet the $1,000 spending requirement and don't need an introductory APR offer, the new VentureOne - Miles Boost offer is the more rewarding option. Its 40,000-mile bonus is worth $740 at TPG's valuations, twice the value of the standard offer.

However, the standard VentureOne may be a better fit if you want an introductory 0% APR period on purchases and balance transfers (for 15 months, then 18.74%-28.74% variable APR; a balance transfer fee applies) or prefer a lower spending requirement.

Whichever offer you choose, you'll get the same ongoing earning rates, redemption options and card benefits without paying an annual fee.

For more information, read our full review of the Capital One VentureOne Rewards.

#6104. So Many People Need Flights To See Dying Loved Ones That A Charity Has Paused New U.S. Requests—Your Miles Can Help

Give A Mile says it’s had to temporarily stop accepting new U.S. flight applications because it doesn’t have the miles and funding to keep up. The people asking for help are trying to reach loved ones in hospice or critical care. Some won’t have another chance to make the trip. If you have United MileagePlus miles you can spare, please help someone get there in time. I’ve supported Give A Mile with my own miles and money, and I serve on their U.S. board. Give A Mile tells me it expects to provide more than 200 flights this year, up from 164 last year. But it’s received more than 1,000 applications. In just the first nine days of November, 80 applications came in, 61 involving the United States. One of the people they’ve helped is Dale, who needed to get from Bismarck to San Francisco after his father went into hospice following surgery. He couldn’t afford the airfare, and driving wasn’t practical. A health care worker suggested Give A Mile. Give A Mile collects donated miles in its own account and uses them to book actual award tickets. Their volunteers review requests, obtain medical confirmation and arrange the flights. The organization also covers the ticket’s taxes and fees. Their holiday campaign aims to provide 50 flights. You don’t need enough miles to fund an entire ticket. Donations are pooled, so 1,000 or 5,000 miles can help complete an award that gets someone on a plane. United’s current minimum donation is just 100 miles. If you’ve got a small MileagePlus balance you haven’t found a use for, or a larger one you can spare some of, I’d appreciate your help. Donate United miles to Give A Mile here. You can also donate Aeroplan points or cash which helps cover very modest expenses like taxes and fees, the organization’s insurance and bookkeeping costs, and occasionally buying tickets when award redemption doesn’t make sense. Gary, I checked out the Give-A-Mile website. It’s nice to see that United isn’t the only airline participating, but it would be nice if the other airlines had lower minimum transfer amounts. It would be great if the other airlines dropped their minimums to either 1000 or 2500 miles for the month of December. People are in a giving mood, charities make year-end appeals, and the other airlines could generate a bit of positive PR. This program deserves far more public awareness than it has now.

Sorry, Gary… fine cause, but (and I say this each time) these airlines should be donating these and/or actually providing real bereavement rates (many of them are inflated, worse than the market price even), not guilt tripping the rest of us.

@1990 – the airline isn’t guilt tripping anyone, United allows charities to accept and spend miles rather than prohibiting it like most carriers do

@Gary Leff — Well then, United’s ahead of most peers on letting charities actually use miles. (@Tim Dunn, shouldn’t Delta step it up?)

#6102. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6100. A Top Frequent Flyer Complained About American Airlines Selling Their Free Upgrade For $91—Gets Told To Delete Their Post

An American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits. The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending. But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.” We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending.

But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

@rawdbee We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026

The important takeaway here is that upgrades are mostly dead, that this is generally true across major U.S. carriers, but hiding this isn’t the reason American Airlines asks this customer to delete their tweet.

If this passenger is shocked by $91 upgrade offers, wait till they learn about American Airlines selling upgrades to infrequent customers for $40 (or Delta Delta doing it for $26) rather than honoring the promised complimentary benefit. And wait until they learn that pilots have priority over them too while deadheading.

Of course American Airlines “genuinely appreciate[s]” a customer’s loyalty when they’re being given business by someone based on the promise of an upgrade benefit that they don’t actually need to deliver, selling their excess seats for tens of dollars rather than providing those seats the way they traditionally did as a perk for someone that’s provided tens of thousands of dollars of business. They appreciate the customer sticking around even when they’re no longer delivering the perks.

Lest you think this is uniquely an American Airlines issue, not only have I seen Delta upsell seats for even less than American (on both domestic and long haul international routes), but United Airlines was equally a pioneer of the technique – they used to pitch infrequent flyers not just on the upgrade itself but that a paid upgrade would leapfrog them over a loyal customer.

I imagine – though American failed to explain this – the reason they’d suggest removing the tweet is because the image of the passenger’s reservation includes the reservation number. A bad actor who sees it might use it to social engineer access to the booking and make changes. It’s not advisable to publicly post a “PNR” (passenger name record) on the internet even if probably nobody does anything with it. Airlines generally tell customers their status upgrades are no longer available on the cheapest (basic economy) fares. Frontier Airlines is introducing first class, but saying even their top Diamond members will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades if they spend extra by buying a bundle. Elites are asked to purchase a lottery ticket on top of their regular ticket for the change of an upgrade, in a game that’s rigged because the airline determines whether there’s a prize at all (narrator: there usually isn’t). My issue isn’t the airline’s right to make this decision that they value $40 from a one a year flyer over rewarding the loyalty of a $30,000 a year customer, or someone spending $200,000 or more on an airline’s credit card (though this may be unwise). Instead, it’s the disconnect between the airline’s marketing and what they now actually deliver. Airlines promise upgrades as a benefit of customer loyalty. For many decades they delivered this. Now they not only fail to deliver it the way they did in the past, that failure is intentional, traded for minor ducats from low value flyers. Earlier this year, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom spoke to investors and explained the strategy selling buy ups instead of giving out free upgrades in the same merchandising category as “pre-purchase bags, checked baggage.” Twenty years ago 90% of first class seats went to upgrades and awards. Ten years ago it was about half. Now only around 12% of seats are left for Delta SkyMiles elite members. And that means on many routes and flights there are no upgrades at all. The real effect of this is to make top status unappealing. It removes upgrades as the argument for status, and that used to be the main motivator. It’s mid-tier status that’s now the sweet spot: priority check-in (shorter lines with bags) priority boarding (overhead bin space) free checked bags extra legroom coach seat The value in being at the top of the list of flyers that do not clear for an upgrade is minimal. Still, the extra value in top status is not zero. I value being able to add an extra segment to an American Airlines itinerary as a backup when my flights are delayed, without having to make the decision to switch flights right away. For many flyers that’s pretty niche. For most it’s not worth chasing. Delta works to convince flyers that extra legroom economy seats are an upgrade (“The biggest trick the devil in Atlanta ever played was convincing flyers he doesn’t exist”). They even run an upgrade process to get into those seats. But that just reinforces the notion that status which is sufficient to get into these extra legroom seats is all you need to work to attain. The problem for airlines isn’t just that this reduces the incentive for their best customers to keep flying with them. It’s that elite members are the ones most likely to get and spend on their credit cards. And they’ve been leaning into status as the biggest reason for these customers to focus their spending this way. What I’d like to see is airlines return to offering meaningful benefits even in the face of monetizing unsold first class seats for tens of dollars to once a year customers. They could offer a discount on paid upgrades in lieu of complimentary upgrades. American Airlines will already discount their tickets, including award tickets, all day long – employees and family members can book ‘AA20’ fares for 20% off. Other airlines have similar programs. So offering upgrades at 20% off for elites could make real sense. Similarly, cobrand cardmembers at Delta and United get discounts on award redemption (at Delta this is really just charging non-cardmembers more). That model could be replicated with upgrades. They could bring back middle seat blocking on flights that aren’t full, keeping the seats next to top elite members empty until they’re actually needed at the gate. That’s easier to manage now that much of gate work is being automated. I use a $70 per hour rubric on whether it was worth paying to upgrade, though this is dependent on whether I think I’ll get the upgrade free, anyway (and the cheaper the upgrade, the more likely the airline thinks they won’t sell the seat) and what seat I already have (an exit row aisle makes me less likely to pay than a middle seat in back of regular coach). The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings. The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings. #6099. Privatize Air Traffic Control

A plane takes off from Hollywood Burbank Airport in Burbank, Calif., October 7, 2025.

Thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving. Otherwise, Steve Martin and John Candy’s long trek home would have become a near-universal experience.

Over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop. No plane was allowed to take off from a U.S. airport for over four hours. The stoppage was necessary when the FAA’s telecommunications network suddenly failed, apparently caused by a faulty update to its decades-old tangle of copper wiring.

This was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. The previous one happened less than four years ago, in January 2023, and was also caused by technical difficulties. Republican lawmakers blamed the Biden administration last time; now, Democrats are faulting the Trump administration. But the FAA’s antiquated infrastructure isn’t a partisan issue. It’s the institutional consequence of having an unaccountable bureaucracy manage the skies.

Unlike almost every other major country, the U.S. federal government funds and operates air traffic control directly. Congress must appropriate its budget each year, and controllers must work without pay when the government shuts down. Infrastructure investments are subject to political timetables. Meanwhile, the FAA is expected to regulate the very system that it runs.

Usually, it wastes no time in dodging responsibility. Immediately after the grounding, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — who oversees the FAA as part of his department — placed the blame on Congress and past administrations for not adequately funding upgrades to the agency’s aging infrastructure. Yet the FAA received $12.5 billion from last year’s reconciliation law for that purpose. Earlier this month, it requested $30 billion more. Now, Duffy claims that he really needs $50 billion to get the job done. And we thought airlines’ add-on fees were bad.

Improvements don’t have to be so costly. The FAA has spent a quarter century trying to switch its network from copper wires to fiber-optic cables. Its counterpart up north, Nav Canada, completed most of the same transition in just 18 months.

The fundamental difference? Nav Canada was spun off from the national government in 1996 as a nonprofit corporation. The organization is funded entirely by user fees from the airlines and private aircraft that rely on its systems, not general taxes, and it’s structured to be accountable to both private stakeholders and the government. When it needs to finance capital projects, Nav Canada doesn’t have to wait for approval. It can simply issue bonds and recoup the cost over the long run.

The results are impressive. Research finds that privatization lowered costs and boosted productivity for the aviation sector, especially compared with the FAA. Safety has greatly improved, and Nav Canada leads in technological advancement. Dozens of countries have since followed Canada’s lead toward an independent, commercial operator.

Passengers wait at a terminal after the FAA issued a national ground stop following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 2026.

America almost joined that list in 2017. That year, legislation gained traction in Congress that would have transferred air traffic control to an independent entity while retaining the FAA’s oversight role. Regrettably, the plan was shot down by the labor union representing controllers, which feared losing the federal government’s generous protections and benefits. Private aircraft owners also opposed it to avoid paying user fees they are currently exempt from, keeping the revenue burden on commercial flyers.

Aside from placating these entrenched interests, there is no good reason to keep air traffic control in government hands. The public utility model has proven safe and effective elsewhere, and the FAA has shown once again that it can’t measure up. Free the aviation system from political gamesmanship, and watch dependability soar.

#6098. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6097. A Trick To Buy Accor Hotel Stays At 40% Off — And Black Friday May Make It Even Better

Loyalty Lobby flagged Accor’s pre-Black Friday subscription sale. Combined with a weakened Brazilian currency this creates an opportunity.

Accor is much bigger than its presence in the United States would have you think. The French hotel company finished September with 5,857 hotels and 885,219 rooms. They operate in more than 110 countries, with a huge presence in Europe and extensive coverage in Asia and Australia.

Their brands include Fairmont, Raffles, Sofitel and MGallery at the luxury end, along with Swissôtel, Pullman and Mövenpick. Then there are Novotel and Mercure, and the budget ibis brands. U.S. options include Fairmont Austin and Raffles Boston.

I took advantage of the Bilt status match I wrote about this summer, which offered up to Platinum.

Accor points are worth 2 euro cents apiece toward eligible hotel stays. The familiar redemption is 2,000 points for €40. Using November 18 exchange rates, that’s about $43.87, or 2.19 U.S. cents per point.

There’s no hotel award chart. An expensive room requires more points. But you can apply points to paid rates without hunting for a limited supply of standard award rooms, and a lower room rate means fewer points needed also.

Reward points normally expire after 12 months without eligible earning activity. A qualifying points credit extends the whole balance, even if you earn just one point. Partner earning can keep the account alive without another hotel stay. An active ALL Signature subscription also protects Reward points from expiration.

Here’s the calculation using the published monthly prices multiplied by 12, less 20%, and November 18 exchange rates. Dollar amounts are rounded.

Your card’s conversion rate will also differ slightly, and be sure to use a card without foreign transaction fees.

The Explorer plan is the better pure points purchase. You’re buying hotel credit for about 29.8% below its redemption value, compared with 23.8% for Absolute. Absolute buys more points and more status credit, but each redeemable point costs more.

Unfortunately, annual payment doesn’t make all the points available immediately. Absolute deposits 5,000 points a month, plus another 5,000 every fourth month, for 75,000 over 12 months. Explorer delivers 3,000 monthly plus 3,000 every fourth month, totaling 45,000. You can’t sign up and immediately spend the full year’s balance on a hotel booking.

You can stack this with ALL Accor+ Explorer, a separate paid membership offering 15% off eligible rates at participating hotels worldwide, plus benefits concentrated in Asia Pacific. Accor uses “Explorer” for both a Signature subscription tier and a different membership. Apparently someone thought that was a good idea.

Buying discounted points and then spending them against an eligible discounted room rate is where this gets better. Combining a 15% room discount with points purchased 29.8% below face value produces about 40.3% off the underlying room price, before the separate membership cost and the rewards you’d otherwise earn.

Signature’s monthly Status points are separate from its redeemable Reward points. Absolute supplies 1,000 Status points a month, or 12,000 over a full year, versus the 14,000 needed for Platinum. Those points count in the calendar year they’re credited and reset at year end.

There’s also an escape valve if your hotel plans change: Accor points transfer to airlines.

Many other partners offer a worse ratio. British Airways, for instance, takes 4,000 Accor points for just 2,000 Avios. Use Iberia for Avios rather than accepting half as many through British Airways.

At the Explorer subscription price above, you’re acquiring points for about 1.54 cents each. That’s also the acquisition cost of a mile through a 1:1 transfer. But once you have the points, moving them to an airline means giving up about 2.19 cents each in hotel credit.

#6096. Let’s Stop Fighting Gravity in U.S.-Canada Trade

Canada needs the United States. But the U.S. also needs, and greatly benefits from, its relationship with Canada in both trade and security.

A transport truck drives towards Canada at the Canada-U.S. border crossing in Fort Erie Ontario, Canada, April 2, 2025.

U.S.-Canada trade is a little like gravity. You can push against it, but the size and proximity of the U.S. economy and the convenience of a G-7 market like Canada always pull us back together.

Trade negotiations between the two countries had been suspended, but the midterm results may be an opportunity to press forward as Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and Senate shift the political calculus. President Donald Trump seemed to warm to the idea of a deal on the campaign trail. Some analysts are suggesting a deal is imminent, and Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadian and U.S. teams would be working to deliver a deal “in the coming weeks” following a “good conversation” with Trump.

Hendrik Brakel is the former chief economist of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and former chief economic adviser to the leader of Canada’s Official Opposition.

Daniel Dorman is the managing editor and director of operations at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa.

On “Let’s Stop Fighting Gravity in U.S.-Canada Trade”

#6094. FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas. Now the story is becoming about Elon Musk: a claim that DOGE cut FAA employees, oversight was loosened, and this led to the flight stoppage. There’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE. A Router Change Disrupted The National Network The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it shows the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges users and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The new $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions. One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo.

According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.)

Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change.

One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981.

Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date.

There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop.
